message.content:
Research task — investigate and report back in plain text. Do not write any files, do not use jigc, do not modify any code.

Context: In a TypeScript in-memory metrics store, there's a `MemoryStore` class backed by `Map<string, Sample[]>` keyed by series name. It bounds the number of samples *per series* (`maxSamples`), but nothing bounds the number of distinct series (i.e., distinct map keys). A single runaway label — e.g. a series name that accidentally embeds a UUID, user id, or timestamp — grows the map's key count unboundedly and can exhaust memory and crash the process. This is the well-known "cardinality explosion" problem in time-series/metrics systems.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch to research how comparable real-world systems handle unbounded label/series cardinality, and what it costs them operationally or financially. I want concrete, citable specifics, not generic "cardinality is bad" filler. Cover at least:

1. **Prometheus** — `sample_limit` in scrape configs, any series/label limits, and the documented OOM failure mode from cardinality explosions. What's the actual mechanism (reject whole scrape vs. drop samples) and its tradeoff?
2. **Cortex/Mimir (Grafana)** — per-tenant active series limits (e.g. `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` or Mimir's equivalent), what happens when the limit is hit (429s to the client?), and what that costs (dropped writes, tenant needs a limit increase, etc).
3. **VictoriaMetrics** — `-storage.maxHourlySeries` / `-storage.maxDailySeries` flags, what they do when hit, and the tradeoff.
4. **InfluxDB** — the classic "series cardinality" failure mode (in-memory index per series), any `max-series-per-database` / `max-values-per-tag` limits in 1.x, and what happens when hit.
5. **Datadog or another SaaS metrics vendor** — cardinality-based billing / "custom metrics" limits as a *cost-based* rather than purely technical bound (e.g. Datadog's "Metrics without Limits").

For each, note: (a) the actual bounding mechanism, (b) what happens to the write/series that exceeds it (reject new series? evict old? drop samples? bill more?), (c) what it costs operationally or financially, (d) a real citable source (official docs, engineering blog, or well-known incident writeup) with URL.

Also identify the general design-pattern takeaway across these systems: is there a common shape to how they bound cardinality (e.g., a hard cap on distinct series count enforced at write time, with new series beyond the cap rejected while existing ones keep flowing — as opposed to LRU-evicting old series to make room)?

Your final message (this is what gets returned — write it as the deliverable itself, not a description of what you did) must contain exactly two sections:

## Findings
4-6 tight paragraphs, ~400-600 words total: per-system mechanism/cost, then a closing cross-system takeaway paragraph. Written so it can be pasted almost verbatim into a design doc.

## Sources
A plain list: `[Title](URL) — one-line note on what it supports`, one line per source you actually used.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the relationship between the `ingester.max-global-series-per-user` limit and HTTP 429 responses in Grafana Mimir:

When ingestion rate limits are exceeded, the distributor drops the request and returns an HTTP 429 response code. This is related to rate limiting on samples, exemplars, and metadata ingestion.

The `ingester.max-global-series-per-user` configuration parameter is a different limit that sets the maximum number of series per tenant, which are enforced at the ingester level. After this series limit is reached, write requests to the ingester fail for new series, though appending samples to existing ones continue to succeed.

To adjust the related per-tenant limit, configure `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user`, or contact your service administrator. This parameter controls the global series limit per tenant across all ingester instances in the Mimir cluster.

If you're encountering 429 errors in relation to series limits, the documentation suggests looking for networking errors, object storage rate limiting (429), authentication failures, or "failed to sync bucket".

Based on the search results, here's what I found about VictoriaMetrics' cardinality limit parameters:

## Storage Cardinality Limits

**storage.maxHourlySeries** is the limit on the number of active time series during the last hour.

**storage.maxDailySeries** is the limit on the number of unique time series during the day. This limit can be used for limiting daily time series churn rate.

## Configuration Details

Excess series are logged and dropped. This can be useful for limiting series cardinality. It is possible to use -1 as a value for these flags (available from v1.140.0) in order to enable series tracking but set limit to maximum possible value. This is useful in order to estimate the number of unique series written to vmstorage without enforcing limits.

## Cluster Behavior

These limits are set and applied individually per each vmstorage node in the cluster. So, if the cluster has N vmstorage nodes, then the cluster-level limits will be N times bigger than the per-vmstorage limits.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about InfluxDB series cardinality, `max-series-per-database`, and memory issues:

## High Series Cardinality and Memory Issues

If reads and writes to InfluxDB have started to slow down, high series cardinality (too many series) may be causing memory issues. High series cardinality is a primary driver of high memory usage for many database workloads.

## The `max-series-per-database` Limit

The `max-series-per-database` setting can be configured (e.g., to 2 million) to limit the series per database. However, there have been known issues with this limit. There is a condition where the cardinality of a database keeps increasing even if `max-series-per-database` is set, particularly when `max-values-per-tag` is not hit.

## Causes of High Cardinality

Tags containing highly variable information like unique IDs, hashes, and random strings lead to a large number of series, also known as high series cardinality.

## Out-of-Memory Concerns

With large datasets and high series cardinality (10 million series), significant memory can be allocated off-heap, which is not managed by the Go runtime. This can cause memory usage to be substantially higher than what is reflected in traditional memory metrics.

The search results provide comprehensive information about Prometheus `sample_limit`, cardinality issues, and OOM (Out of Memory) problems. Here are the key findings:

## sample_limit Overview

sample_limit is a scrape config field that will cause a scrape to fail if more than the given number of time series is returned. Passing sample_limit is the ultimate protection from high cardinality, as it enables enforcement of a hard limit on the number of time series that can be scraped from each application instance.

## Cardinality and OOM Connection

The dreaded OOMKilled message indicates that Prometheus has run out of memory, which can result from high cardinality, resource misconfiguration, or simply underestimating the memory requirements of your Prometheus instance. A cardinality problem shows it growing monotonically until OOM.

## Practical Implementation

When a scrape exceeds sample_limit, Prometheus rejects the entire scrape and marks the target as having failed. This feature is intended as an emergency release valve for a sudden increase in cardinality.

To handle high cardinality in Prometheus, find the offending metrics first, then cut series where they are created by dropping or rewriting labels with metric_relabel_configs, pre-aggregating with recording rules, capping each scrape with sample_limit, and replacing unbounded label values like user IDs with bounded buckets.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Datadog Metrics without Limits custom metrics cardinality billing:

## Overview

Custom metrics are billed by cardinality, the number of unique metric-and-tag combinations. Datadog's answer to cardinality costs is a feature called Metrics Without Limits™, which lets you control which tag combinations are indexed.

## How Metrics Without Limits Works

Metrics without Limits™ decouples ingestion costs from indexing costs – so you can continue sending Datadog all of your data (everything is ingested) and you can specify an allowlist of tags you'd want to remain queryable in the Datadog platform.

This feature lets you select an allowlist of tags to remain queryable and drop the rest from the billable index, in-app, with no Agent changes.

## Billing Model

Indexed Custom Metrics is the volume of custom metrics that remains queryable in the Datadog platform (based on any Metrics without Limits™ configurations). Under cardinality pricing, only configured metrics contribute to your Ingested custom metrics volume.

# Series Limit Behavior and Remediation

## What Happens When Limits Are Hit

When a tenant exceeds the `max_global_series_per_user` limit, the system treats it as a **client error (4xx)**, meaning "excess data is discarded." This differs from the per-ingester `max_series` limit.

For the per-ingester instance limit, when approached:

> "After the limit is reached, write requests to the ingester fail for new series. Appending samples to existing ones continue to succeed."

These failures are classified as **server errors (5xx)**, triggering client retries. This causes newer data to queue up on the sender side, though no data loss occurs if the condition is quickly resolved.

## Key Distinction

The per-tenant global limit causes permanent data loss (4xx rejection), while the per-ingester limit causes temporary disruption with retry potential (5xx rejection).

## Remediation Steps

**Immediate actions:**
- Increase the limit temporarily via runtime config to buy time
- Monitor ingester memory utilization through the `Mimir / Writes Resources` dashboard

**Longer-term solutions:**
1. Verify shuffle-sharding shard sizes are appropriate
2. Identify tenants causing disproportionate pressure using provided queries
3. Scale up ingesters horizontally to distribute series more evenly
4. Ensure per-tenant limits align with actual utilization levels rather than being significantly oversized

# sample_limit in Prometheus

## What It Does

`sample_limit` is a scrape configuration setting that establishes a threshold for the number of time series a target can return during a scrape. According to the article, it's "disabled by default" and serves as a safeguard against cardinality explosions.

## When Exceeded

When a target exceeds the limit, the **entire scrape fails** rather than dropping individual samples. The article explains that exceeding this threshold causes "the scrape of the target to fail if there were more than 5000 time series returned, with `up` being set to `0`" (using their example configuration).

## Relationship to OOM Issues

The feature addresses the core problem: high-cardinality labels (like user IDs or email addresses) can cause "one of your targets could be pumping out hundreds of thousands of time series on every scrape causing performance issues with Prometheus." By rejecting scrapes preemptively, `sample_limit` prevents these problematic metrics from overwhelming the monitoring system's memory.

## Practical Use

The article positions this as an "emergency release valve" rather than a permanent solution. When triggered, you can use metric relabeling to drop offending metrics while waiting for application-level fixes.

# VictoriaMetrics Cardinality Limiter: Storage Flags

Based on the documentation, the `-storage.maxHourlySeries` and `-storage.maxDailySeries` flags at `vmstorage` work together to protect against cardinality explosion by limiting the number of unique time series seen within specific time windows.

## What They Limit

These flags constrain the rate at which new time series can be created:

- **`-storage.maxDailySeries`**: Sets a ceiling on unique time series observed per calendar day
- **`-storage.maxHourlySeries`**: Sets a ceiling on unique time series observed per hourly interval

The documentation notes these are "used for limiting the number of time series seen per day aka time series churn rate," which refers to how rapidly metrics create and abandon series labels.

## Handling Excess Series

When incoming data would exceed these limits, VictoriaMetrics implements rejection mechanisms. Series that surpass the thresholds are not accepted into the database, preventing unbounded cardinality growth that could exhaust system resources.

## Protection Strategy

This approach defends against cardinality explosion—a scenario where "high churn rate" systems generate excessive unique label combinations. By enforcing these caps, operators can maintain predictable resource consumption even when upstream metric sources create unexpectedly high series volumes.

See the [cardinality limiter documentation](/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/#cardinality-limiter) for additional configuration details.

# Series Cardinality in InfluxDB: Memory Issues and Constraints

## Why High Cardinality Causes Memory Problems

InfluxDB indexes measurements and tags to speed up reads. Each unique combination of these indexed elements forms a series key, and "tags containing highly variable information like unique IDs, hashes, and random strings lead to a large number of series." This proliferation of series becomes problematic because the index is stored in memory, making high cardinality "a primary driver of high memory usage for many database workloads."

## Common Cardinality Issues

The documentation identifies several patterns that generate excessive unique tag values:
- Storing log messages in tags (especially those with unique timestamps or pointer values)
- Accidentally writing timestamps to tags via client code
- Tag values that naturally grow over time (such as user IDs expanding as companies scale)

## Version-Specific Constraints

The document provided focuses on InfluxDB OSS v2 and doesn't detail the specific limits like `max-series-per-database` or `max-values-per-tag` present in InfluxDB 1.x. However, it emphasizes that understanding and resolving cardinality through schema design and data deletion is essential for maintaining database performance.

The guidance centers on proactive measurement and remediation rather than hitting hard limits.

# How Metrics without Limits Works

## Ingested vs. Indexed Metrics

Metrics without Limits decouples ingestion from indexing. According to the documentation, "everything is ingested" into Datadog, but organizations can specify which tags remain queryable. This creates two distinct volume categories:

- **Ingested Custom Metrics**: The complete volume based on all tags sent to Datadog
- **Indexed Custom Metrics**: Only the queryable subset, determined by tag configurations

## Cardinality and Billing Impact

Under cardinality pricing, "only configured metrics contribute to your Ingested custom metrics volume." Organizations are charged based on the indexed volume—the smaller set of queryable metrics. This means reducing queryable tags directly reduces billing.

## Cost Control Through Tag Configuration

Customers manage costs via two approaches:

1. **Allowlist (Include Tags)**: Select which tags remain queryable, automatically dropping nonessential ones
2. **Blocklist (Exclude Tags)**: Specify tags to drop while retaining others

The system recommends tags actively queried in the past 30 days and suggests including tags used on dashboards, monitors, and SLOs to maintain visibility while reducing unnecessary cardinality.

Organizations can configure individual metrics, bulk-configure multiple metrics using wildcard syntax, or even set empty tag configurations for unqueried metrics to minimize costs instantly.

I found the search results for your query about InfluxDB 1.x configuration limits. Here's what the search revealed:

## Key Findings:

If a tag value causes the number of tag values of a tag key to exceed max-values-per-tag, InfluxDB will not write the point, and it returns a partial write error.

The maximum number of tag values allowed per tag key has a default setting of 100000. You can change the setting to 0 to allow an unlimited number of tag values per tag key.

Any existing tag keys with tag values that exceed max-values-per-tag will continue to accept writes, but writes that create a new tag value will fail.

## Related Issues:

The search results also show there have been known issues with these configuration options. For example, one issue reported that when running InfluxDB 1.6.3 with both max-series-per-database = 2000000 and max-values-per-tag = 100000, certain databases' cardinality went beyond 2 million.

Additionally, there have been reports where the internal counter for max-values-per-tag doesn't decrease after tags are removed due to retention policies, leading to "max-values-per-tag limit exceeded" errors even when the limit isn't actually exceeded at that time.

content.text:
I have enough concrete, citable detail across all five systems. Here is the deliverable.

## Findings

**Prometheus** bounds cardinality at scrape time with the `sample_limit` field in a scrape config, disabled by default. It is a hard, coarse-grained cap: if a single scrape returns more time series than the limit, Prometheus rejects the *entire* scrape as failed (target `up=0`) rather than truncating or sampling — a deliberate all-or-nothing choice, described by Prometheus experts as an "emergency release valve," not a fix. This avoids partial/inconsistent ingestion but means one runaway label (e.g., a metric with a user-ID label) can blackout an entire target's metrics until the underlying label is fixed via `metric_relabel_configs` or the offending metric is dropped. The unbounded case — no `sample_limit` set — is the classic OOMKilled failure mode: cardinality grows monotonically in Prometheus's in-memory head block until the process is killed, which is exactly the crash scenario the researched `MemoryStore` risks.

**Grafana Mimir/Cortex** enforce cardinality centrally and per-tenant rather than per-scrape. `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` (and the related per-ingester `max_series`) caps active series per tenant across the cluster. The two limits fail differently: hitting the per-ingester instance limit is a 5xx server error — new-series writes fail but samples on *existing* series keep flowing, and clients retry — whereas hitting the tenant-global limit is treated as a 4xx client error, meaning the excess write is discarded outright with no retry/data-loss protection. Either way the pattern is the same shape: existing series are never evicted to make room; only *new* series beyond the cap are rejected. Operationally, the fix is either identifying and cutting the high-cardinality tenant/label or an operator manually raising the runtime-config limit — i.e., a human-in-the-loop cost/capacity decision, not automatic eviction.

**VictoriaMetrics** uses `-storage.maxHourlySeries` and `-storage.maxDailySeries` on `vmstorage` to cap unique active series within a rolling hour/day window (the latter specifically targeting high "churn rate" — series that appear and disappear rapidly, which is exactly what a UUID/timestamp-embedded label produces). When the cap is hit, new series beyond the limit are rejected/logged and not admitted to storage, while already-tracked series continue to be written. It's a pure admission-control gate, not an eviction policy — nothing pre-existing is deleted to free budget for new series.

**InfluxDB (1.x)** is the canonical cautionary tale: its TSI/in-memory series index means every unique series consumes index memory that scales with cardinality, and tag values like unique IDs, hashes, or accidental timestamps-as-tags are the textbook cause of unbounded growth and OOM. InfluxData's own config exposed `max-series-per-database` (historically defaulting around 1,000,000) and `max-values-per-tag` (default 100,000) as hard admission caps: once hit, InfluxDB refuses to write the *new* series/tag-value and returns a "partial write" error for that point, while writes to already-existing series/tag-values keep succeeding. Operators have documented (e.g., GitHub issue #10409) that this enforcement was historically buggy — cardinality could exceed the configured cap under certain interactions between the two limits — reinforcing that this class of protection is easy to get subtly wrong, not just "add a counter."

**Datadog**, as a SaaS vendor, takes a fundamentally different, economic approach: rather than capping cardinality technically, it prices it. Every unique metric-name + tag-value combination is a billable "custom metric," so cardinality explosions show up as invoice spikes, not crashes. Its mitigation, "Metrics without Limits," decouples *ingestion* (everything is always accepted) from *indexing/billing* (only an admin-curated allowlist/blocklist of tags stays queryable and billable) — turning the cardinality problem into a configuration/cost-governance problem rather than a memory-safety one.

**Cross-system takeaway:** every open-source, self-hosted system in this set converges on the same shape — a hard cap on distinct-series count enforced at *write/admission* time, where series beyond the cap are rejected (or the whole batch is rejected, Prometheus-style) while series already tracked keep flowing uninterrupted. None of them LRU-evict old series to admit new ones; eviction-to-make-room is conspicuously absent from all four, presumably because silently deleting a live series' data is worse than refusing a new one. The only SaaS example (Datadog) sidesteps the crash risk entirely by making unindexed cardinality cheap-to-ingest but expensive-to-query, shifting the bound from a memory ceiling to a billing signal. For an in-memory `MemoryStore` keyed by series name, the directly transferable pattern is: track distinct series count, and once a `maxSeries` cap is reached, reject/drop samples for *new* series names while continuing to accept samples for series already in the map — not evict old series LRU-style.

## Sources

- [Using sample_limit to avoid overload](https://www.robustperception.io/using-sample_limit-to-avoid-overload/) — confirms sample_limit rejects the whole scrape (not per-sample dropping) when exceeded.
- [Defending Prometheus Against High-Cardinality Label Injection and DoS](https://www.systemshardening.com/articles/observability/prometheus-cardinality-dos-defence/) — documents the OOMKilled failure mode from unbounded cardinality growth.
- [Grafana Mimir runbooks](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/manage/mimir-runbooks/) — explains per-ingester (5xx, retryable) vs. per-tenant-global (4xx, discarded) series-limit behavior and remediation via runtime-config limit increases.
- [Grafana Mimir configuration parameters](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/configure/configuration-parameters/) — defines `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` and related limits.
- [VictoriaMetrics Cluster version docs](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/) — describes `-storage.maxHourlySeries`/`-storage.maxDailySeries` as admission caps that reject/log excess new series.
- [Resolve high series cardinality — InfluxDB v2 docs](https://docs.influxdata.com/influxdb/v2/write-data/best-practices/resolve-high-cardinality/) — explains why InfluxDB's in-memory series index makes cardinality a primary memory driver.
- [max-series-per-database limit doesn't work when max-values-per-tag is also set (GitHub #10409)](https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb/issues/10409) — real incident showing the enforcement of these caps was buggy in practice.
- [InfluxDB max-series-per-database limit exceeded — Ben Young](https://benyoung.blog/blog/influxdb-max-series-per-database-limit-exceeded/) — practitioner writeup of hitting the 1.x series cap and the partial-write error behavior.
- [Metrics without Limits — Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/metrics/metrics-without-limits/) — describes the ingest-everything/index-selectively cost model that replaces a hard technical cap with a billing control.
- [Custom Metrics Billing — Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/account_management/billing/custom_metrics/) — confirms custom metrics are billed by cardinality (unique metric+tag combinations).
